newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Talks on North Korea defector to take time.
newsitem.headline: Talks on North Korea defector to take time.

text.p: China told South Korea on Friday it needs more time to decide what to do about a top North Korean defector now in the South's Beijing embassy, and a Seoul official said no quick action was likely.
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen met for 50 minutes with South Korean counterpart Yoo Chong-ha and said Beijing needed time to investigate.

While Qian gave no indication how much time it may take to sort out the diplomatic crisis, a South Korean official said it was unlikely there would be any action before the two ministers left Singapore after a meeting of Asian and European foreign ministers on Saturday.
"I don't think it's possible," he told Reuters.
The official, who asked not to be identified, added: "It was the begining of a useful discussion, but now it goes into diplomatic channels in Seoul and Beijing."
Qian said the defection of North Korean official Hwang Jang-yop suprised China.
"This incident happened all of a sudden, so we need more time to investigate," Qian told reporters after meeting Yoo.
He urged both Koreas "to treat this matter with a cool and calm manner, to keep peace and stability" as Chinese police surrounded Seoul's embassy in Beijing where Hwang is staying.
Pyongyang says Hwang was kidnapped, an allegation Seoul has dismissed as preposterous.
Yoo told reporters the two sides would meet again, but did not say where or when. He said Friday's talks, which lasted 20 minutes beyond the originally scheduled 30 minutes, were "good".
"Meetings will continue," he added.
Yoo had decided not to attend the Singapore conference after Hwang's defection, then changed his mind so he could meet Qian.
South Korea is urging China to allow Hwang, whom it said arrived by taxi at its embassy on Wednesday with an aide to claim political asylum, to go to Seoul.
North Korea is demanding that China return Hwang, a 73-year-old theoretician credited with devising Pyongyang's quirky brand of socialism.
That leaves Beijing the choice of offending its old socialist comrade or a new capitalist partner that is investing heavily in China's booming economy.

"We did not know what happened to Mr Hwang in Beijing. We were totally in the dark beforehand," Qian said. "We were not aware of his stopover in Beijing. He did not stay at any Chinese hotels or guesthouses."
Western diplomats in Beijing say they believe China has little choice but to respect Hwang's desire to defect.

Some commentators have suggested that Pyongyang, deep in economic trouble and dealing with widespread hunger after disastrous floods, might react violently to the defection of a man who is ranked 24th in its hierarchy.
U.S. officials said the defection was another sign of strains in the Stalinist country that were also reflected in food shortages and reduced military training.
U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said there was no indication of heightened military alert along the border between the two Koreas over the incident.
